extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literary narrative theory; literary critics and advanced creative-writing practitioners studying narrative form
extracted.subtask_description: A framework for analyzing literary narrative discourse by distinguishing story, narrative, and narrating and by investigating three major fields (tense, mood, voice) with attention to temporal relations (order, duration, frequency) and narrating instance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-level distinction: story / narrative / narrating
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'story' for the signified or narrative content (histoire/diegesis), 'narrative' for the signifier/statement/discourse (the narrative text itself), and 'narrating' for the producing action (narration) and the real or fictional situation in which that action takes place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always keep these three terms univocal: story = events recounted (may be fictional or real); narrative = the textual discourse available to analysis; narrating = the act that produces the discourse (which may be fictionalized, e.g., Ulysses telling adventures). Examples: Ulysses' recounted adventures (story) vs the narrative discourse that recounts them; Proust's Recherche: both story and narrating are fictional and must be inferred from the narrative alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic focus on relationships among the three levels
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze the relationships between narrative and story, between narrative and narrating, and, where inscribed, between story and narrating—since textual analysis has direct access only to the narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because events and the narrating act (when fictional) are knowable only indirectly via the narrative, analysis should prioritize how the narrative mediates knowledge of story and narrating (e.g., indicators like first-person pronouns, tense forms, or other indices that signal narrating). External biographical documents cannot substitute for this textual mediation in fictional works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt three analytic fields: tense, mood, voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize narrative analysis into three classes: (1) tense — temporal relations between story and discourse; (2) mood — modalities/degrees of representation (forms of mimesis, point of view, showing vs telling); (3) voice — the narrative situation or instance (narrator and audience, real or implied).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These fields determine the arrangement of chapters and analyses: tense covers order/duration/frequency; mood gathers what Todorov called aspect and parts of mood (point of view, representation); voice covers narrating instance and its protagonists. Do not hypostatize these as substances but treat them as relational fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tense broken into order, duration, frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: Within 'tense', study (a) order — relations between sequence of events in story and their arrangement in narrative; (b) duration — relation between story-duration and narrative-duration (speed); (c) frequency — relations between repetition in story and repetition in narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each of these determinations is a separate axis of temporal analysis: Order is treated via anachronies (see analepsis/prolepsis), Duration examines compression/expansion (e.g., three years summed in two sentences), and Frequency inspects iterative or repetitive narration practices. Use textual examples (e.g., Proust, Iliad) to illustrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish story-time (erz?hlte Zeit) and narrative-time (Erz?hlzeit / pseudo-time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize the dual temporality: the time of the events told (story time) and the time of the narrative discourse (narrative time or 'pseudo-time'), and consider how narrative invents one time-scheme in terms of the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat narrative time as a quasi-fictional or metonymic time that stands for reading/consuming time; be sensitive to medium differences (film and oral narrative more freely manipulate pseudo-time; written texts remain linearly constrained). Consider implications for temporal distortions and reading experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify anachronies: analepsis and prolepsis
rubrics_metrics.description: Any discordance between story-order and narrative-order is an anachrony; designate retrospections as analepses and anticipations as prolepses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pinpoint and measure anachronies by reconstructing story-order when possible; recognize that classical narrative frequently uses anachrony (in medias res, retrograde movements). Examples: the Iliad's opening sequence and Proust's zigzagging fragment. Use formulaic notation (e.g., A4-B5-C3-D2-E1) to summarize sequential relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish subjective vs objective retrospections/anticipations
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate whether a retrospection or anticipation is adopted by a character's consciousness (subjective) or by the narrative/ narrator (objective); note that this distinction is not strictly temporal but relates to mood/point of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark subjective analepses/prolepses when the narrative reports a character's memory or anticipation ('he remembered ...'); mark objective ones when the text/narrator presents the temporal displacement independently. Genette advises neutral terminology for sequence (analepsis/prolepsis) and reserves subjective/objective distinctions for mood analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntactic-sequential method: number sections, assign temporal positions, and map embedment
rubrics_metrics.description: Segment the narrative into distinct sections, assign each a temporal story-position (e.g., 1=earlier, 2=now), and represent subordination/coordination with brackets/parentheses to show embedding of analepses/prolepses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example notation: A2[B1]C2[D1(E2)F1(G2)H1]I2; openings of brackets correspond to dynamic displacements (analepses/prolepses), closings to returns. This exposes hierarchical relations among sections beyond mere positional labeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat narrative as a linguistic 'expansion of a verb'
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceive of narrative as the amplification (rhetorical expansion) of a verbal nucleus (e.g., 'I walk', 'Pierre has come') — even minimal verbal forms can be treated as narratives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This grammatical metaphor justifies organizing narrative problems (tense, mood, voice) with reference to verb grammar and rhetorical amplification; it legitimizes analyzing large works as extended developments of simple verbal statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep narrating act central: narrating produces the discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that the narrative discourse is produced by an act of telling; in some cases (fictive narrators) the act of narrating is constitutive of the events' apparent existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish authorial enunciation from fictional narrating (e.g., Homer vs Ulysses; Proust's narrator vs Proust himself). The narrating act may create the fiction of events (if teller is a liar), and analysis should attend to traces of the narrating act inscribed in the discourse (tense, person, indices of enunciation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about medium constraints on temporality
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for how different narrative media constrain or permit temporal manipulations: cinematic and oral narratives can present sequences visually or out of linear order; written texts are linearly constrained even if reading practices can approximate nonlinearity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume perfect parity across media: you can run a film backwards frame by frame but cannot read a text backwards letter by letter without losing textuality. Treat the reading-time metonymy and its consequences carefully in analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminological and methodological caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Use terms (anachrony, analepsis, prolepsis, tense/mood/voice) with awareness of their etymologies and the risk of psychological connotations; prefer neutral terms for temporal sequence and reserve psychological labels for mood/point-of-view discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genette notes conflicts of Greek roots and recommends careful deployment of terminology; keep clear distinctions between temporal categories (tense-related) and perspective/representational categories (mood-related).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that perfect temporal correspondence is hypothetical (zero degree)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume a hypothetical 'zero degree' where narrative-order perfectly corresponds to story-order, but treat it as an ideal benchmark for identifying and classifying anachronies, not as a common default.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the zero-degree as a reference point when pinpointing and measuring anachronies; historical traditions (folklore) may approximate chronological order, but literary practice often embraces anachrony as a formal resource (e.g., in medias res).
